conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting, and there are no right or wrong answers. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. My hope is that this feels like a safe, supportive space where we can figure out together what kind of help or resources might make life feel a little lighter. Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[smiles faintly, then shrugs]

I can still laugh—sometimes. Like, if my husband makes a silly joke while he’s changing her diaper, I’ll chuckle. But it feels… flatter than before she was born. I used to really belly-laugh at things, and now it’s more like a quick “ha” and then I’m back to feeling tired.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod]

Yeah… that’s mostly true for me. I can still laugh, but it’s not as easy or as often. Sometimes I’ll smile at something funny on my phone, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I know I *should* enjoy it, not because it naturally lifts me up the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[glances down at hands]

I do look forward to some things—like my mom coming over tomorrow so I can take a shower without rushing. But bigger stuff, like the brunch my friends planned for next week… I’m not excited the way I used to be. Part of me wants to feel that buzz, but mostly I just feel kind of flat, like I’ll probably go and smile and come home exhausted.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet sigh]

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday she spit up a ton right after I fed her, and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her tummy. My husband said it’s just what babies do, but I still wondered if I’d propped her wrong or ate too much dairy. It’s not every little thing, but when stuff goes sideways I do catch myself wondering what I did to cause it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[twists the edge of her blanket]

Sometimes. Like, I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly think, “What if her breathing sounds weird?” I’ll check her—she’s fine—and I can calm myself down pretty fast, but it still pops up out of nowhere. It’s not every day, but maybe three or four times this week I’ve had that rush of worry without a real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses a hand to chest]

A couple of times, yeah—this sudden tight feeling, like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch a full breath. It only lasts a minute or two, and I tell myself it’s just my body being weird, but in the moment it feels scary even though nothing’s actually wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly]

Some days, yeah. Like when she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up and I need to start dinner—it feels as if everything’s happening at once and I can’t quite keep up. I usually manage to get through it, but I end those days pretty drained and on edge.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[rubs her eyes]

Not really. I can fall asleep okay once my head hits the pillow—it’s actually one of the few times I feel kind of peaceful. Once in a while I’ll lie there going over the day, but mostly I drift off pretty fast.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shrugs, voice soft]

Yeah… I do feel sad some of the time. It’s not every moment, but there are stretches—especially late afternoon—when I just feel kind of heavy and tearful. Yesterday I cried while folding her onesies, and I couldn’t really explain why; it just felt like a cloud sitting on me for a while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes well up a little]

Yes… maybe once or twice this week. Nothing huge happened—I just got overwhelmed, like when she wouldn’t latch and I felt my chest tighten. I put her in the bassinet, stepped into the kitchen, and the tears just came. It passed after a few minutes, but I hate that it keeps happening.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No, never. I might feel low or stressed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her.

Adjusting to new motherhood can feel like riding an emotional roller-coaster, and it sounds as though you've been carrying more lows than highs lately. You shared that laughter comes less easily and feels forced, that activities you once anticipated with joy now seem flat, and that waves of <sym>sadness</sym> and unexplained tears arrive without warning. You're working so hard to stay on top of feedings, housework, and worries about your baby's wellbeing, yet you still blame yourself whenever anything goes wrong. At the same time, sudden <sym>anxiety</sym> and brief <sym>panic</sym> sensations catch you off guard, making an ordinary afternoon feel overwhelming. Your honesty about these feelings is a brave and important step toward getting the right support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient expresses diminished anticipatory pleasure for most events, describing feeling "flat" and lacking the former "buzz"—closest to "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring self-blame for everyday baby issues, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unprovoked worries multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes repeated episodes of sudden racing-heart, breath-catching panic that feel scary despite no external trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent overwhelm ('some days, yeah'), multiple stressors, and feeling drained/on edge, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, noticeable sadness with unexplained crying, mapping to "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you above the 13-point cutoff indicating probable major <med>depressive</med> symptoms with peripartum onset. You endorse <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>no excitement for the brunch</quote>), daily <sym>sadness</sym> (<quote>cloud sitting on me</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym> and <sym>self-reproach</sym>, multiple <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> episodes, and feeling <quote>on edge</quote> when tasks pile up-findings that align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (duration >2 weeks, clinically significant distress). You denied self-harm, so immediate safety concerns are absent, yet functional impairment is evident. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about referral to a perinatal <med>mental health specialist</med> for therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and possible medication if indicated
3. Plan brief daily mood check-ins with your partner or support person; note sleep, appetite, and crying episodes
4. Prioritise rest: accept help with night feeds when possible and aim for at least one four-hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep
5. Add calming micro-breaks-five slow breaths, a short walk, or listening to music-to reduce <sym>overwhelm</sym>
6. Continue to monitor <sym>anxiety</sym> spikes; if they worsen or you notice <sym>panic</sym> symptoms lasting longer, contact your clinician promptly
7. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US) or local equivalent, and your provider's after-hours line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Clinical Note  

**Presenting symptoms endorsed**  
- Low mood with tearfulness, “heavy” feelings, especially late afternoon  
- Marked reduction in pleasure/interest (laughing only with effort, no excitement for social events)  
- Self-blame/guilt when baby has minor problems  
- Recurrent anxious worries (“breathing sounds wrong”) and brief panic-like episodes (3-4×/wk, <2 min)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “on edge” when multiple demands coincide  
- Crying spells (2× this week) without clear precipitant  
- No current sleep-onset difficulties; no self-harm ideation  

**Pattern summary**  
Persistent dysphoria and anhedonia, accompanied by situational guilt, intermittent anxiety/panic, and decreased coping reserve. Episodes of tearfulness and sense of emotional “flatness” are present. No safety concerns voiced.

**Screening significance**  
Findings are consistent with mild-to-moderate postpartum depressive symptoms with co-occurring anxiety; frequency and functional impact warrant follow-up with formal assessment (PHQ-9/EPDS) and clinical interview to determine diagnosis and care options.

**Risk factors noted**  
- Daily sadness and crying  
- Loss of enjoyment  
- Self-blame/guilt  
- Anxiety/panic symptoms  
- Overwhelm with routine tasks  
- Absence of self-harm ideation (protective)

**Plan**  
Provide screening results to patient; schedule follow-up within 1 week for standardized rating scales, psychosocial support review, and possible referral for treatment planning.
